verdicts.rewritten_summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): trans women in France are held in prisons matching the gender marker on their identity documents (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code) — most end up in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them ('we don't want any women here'), placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework applies to the department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of the CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog (25 May 2021): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across ALL French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons plus on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse sites). Covers placement, isolation, safety and staff-training recommendations. Binds the department's prisons as French establishments.

Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Martinique resource page: same-sex acts decriminalised in 1815; Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department; 2013 marriage-equality law applies; discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation prohibited in goods/services since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code arts. 225-1/225-2) and in employment since Labour Code art. L1132-1 (2008); gender-identity discrimination prohibited since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, with 'sexual identity' replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. Also lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts.

JM Concept 972 (French): Martinique's lesbian, gay, bi and trans network provides information, meetings and services to the island's LGBT community and runs private parties and garden parties (site lists 2025 events for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September) with the support of gay-friendly heterosexual supporters. Active, dated evidence of local community infrastructure on the island.

Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: the Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct — advances noted for lesbian, gay and bisexual people with 'less evident' progress for trans or intersex people. No same-sex marriage or civil unions recognised; Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against sexual-orientation discrimination; intersex newborns may be registered 'undetermined' under the 2021 Civil Status Act but nonconsensual intersex procedures are not banned; legal gender recognition not possible and LGBTI organisations cannot register. Pride held since 2005 with counter-protesters; during the 2024 national elections a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and others used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech.

AfricLaw (23 August 2024, Lakshita Kanhiya): analyses the historic participation of Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan — the first transgender woman in Miss Universe Mauritius 2024 — against the country's legal obstacles: the Civil Status Act of 1981 and Central Population Database as the framework denying recognition, plus pervasive stigmatisation, with activism by the Young Queer Alliance and Association VISA-G. Concludes legal recognition and protection for trans Mauritians remain inadequate despite the visibility milestone.

US State Department 2016 Country Report — Mauritius: Section 250 sodomy statute almost never reached same-sex couples in court (sodomy references overwhelmingly arose in heterosexual divorce cases as an aggravating factor); documents societal discrimination, with LGBTI victims of family verbal abuse or violence reporting to local NGOs including Collectif Arc-en-Ciel and Young Queer Alliance, and harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing. Dated pre-2023 baseline for the record.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Human Rights Watch dispatch (11 July 2024): Malawi's Constitutional Court on 28 June 2024 rejected the challenge to Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156 — a three-member panel dismissed the application brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani, a trans woman who received an eight-year sentence in a men's prison in December 2021. The sections carry up to 14 years' imprisonment; faith-based groups filed briefs and religious leaders led nationwide protests claiming the case sought to legalise same-sex marriage. The court left any reform to parliament; HRW called it a 'dark day' and warned of heightened arbitrary-arrest and violence risks.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Human Rights Watch (26 October 2018), releasing the 61-page report 'Let Posterity Judge' based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre plus lawyers, activists and officials: police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people, sometimes assaulting them, and medical staff denied services on gender-expression grounds (a trans man beaten then refused treatment; nurses mocked people presenting for HIV tests). Men face up to 14 years and women five years under sections 153/156; the 2012 justice-minister moratorium on arrests was reaffirmed in December 2015 but suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 after religious leaders' litigation, leaving its legality contested. People whose gender expression differs from expectations are 'most likely to be targeted'.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 December 2015): two men arrested in Malawi on 7 December on homosexuality charges suffered house ransacking and assault by neighbours, threats of being burned alive, attempted extortion and humiliation by community police — forced stripping, forced medical and HIV/STD examinations, and photos distributed on social media. CEDEP's Gift Trapence contrasts the arrests with government Global Fund money for LGBTI HIV services. Documents the arrest-and-abuse pattern under the penal code.

Erasing 76 Crimes (27 April 2018): police arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, in Mzuzu for suspected homosexuality and charged him under section 156 ('indecent practices between males') rather than section 153 — apparently to circumvent the six-year moratorium on anti-gay arrests while both laws faced a constitutional challenge. Police spokespersons confirmed the custody. Evidence of law-enforcement attempts to elude the moratorium.

Human Dignity Trust country profile — Malaysia (live page in cache): federal Penal Code section 377 criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 20 years plus whipping), alongside Sharia enactments across the states prohibiting 'cross-dressing' or 'males posing as females' — including the Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019 covering 'sodomy' and 'sexual intercourse against the order of nature'. Situates Malaysia among jurisdictions that criminalise, with active litigation listed alongside the Mauritius and Namibia cases.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Human Rights Watch report (10 August 2022) 'I Don't Want to Change Myself', based on interviews with 73 LGBT people in Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 across seven states plus journalists and lawyers: every state and the federal territories (Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya) maintain Sharia codes criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity ('a man posing as a woman'), while the federal penal code punishes oral/anal sex with up to 20 years plus mandatory whipping. Government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events/media content were censored. The 2021 Nur Sajat case shows enforcement reach — 122 religious officers were mobilised to hunt her over 'insulting Islam' before she fled to Thailand and gained UNHCR protection.

Human Rights Watch (25 June 2019): a transgender woman was killed in Klang, a Kuala Lumpur suburb — the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months — with the piece documenting violence against trans people alongside police mistreatment and impunity ('The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself').

verdicts.rewritten_summary: The Diplomat (10 December 2025): on 28 November police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B — the largest such raid since 2022 — with media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked, suspending 17 civil servants identified among them. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground under 377B, yet release was delayed; over 130 remained held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang. Documents current enforcement-and-exposure risks against queer spaces, including for foreign visitors.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: International Commission of Jurists (July 2020): Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Mohamad Al-Bakri announced he had given the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) 'full licence to carry out its enforcement actions' against transgender persons; the ICJ condemned the order, demanded its revocation and called for non-discrimination guarantees. Documents state-sanctioned targeting of trans people in the federal territories.

Malaysia4U legal guide (updated July 2026): sections 377A/377B criminalise 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' for any person regardless of gender or consent — maximum 20 years plus whipping — and apply to tourists; state Syariah offences (liwat, musahaqah, cross-dressing) apply only to Muslims (max 3 years, RM5,000 fine, 6 strokes). The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Syariah provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds without decriminalising anything under the Penal Code; enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted. No same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law; sodomy first criminalised in 1871.

Human Rights Watch (24 September 2014) 'I'm Scared to Be a Woman': since the 1980s every one of Malaysia's 13 states has passed Sharia enactments institutionalising discrimination against trans people — all 13 bar Muslim men from 'dressing as women' and three also bar 'women posing as men' — enforced by state Islamic religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing. Documents the 2011 strip-search and sexual assault of Victoria by religious officials, repeated arrests (one woman over 20 times), routine rejection of gender-marker changes by the Registration Department (a 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery), and prison terms of four months to three years with male-ward sexual violence. Follows the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014 that triggered the Negeri Sembilan constitutional challenge (Court of Appeal decision then expected 7 November 2014).

BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018): trans women in France are incarcerated per their identity-document gender (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code), typically in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them, placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework binds this department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL (25 May 2021): 'persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty — based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse). Extends to local jails as French establishments.

LINFO.re (French-language report): the French National Assembly voted the simplification of legal gender change (civil-status change for trans people) — French law applies to the department, bringing the simplified procedure here. Headline-verified in cache; body largely navigation content at fetch time.

Erasing 76 Crimes (23 May 2023, Moïse Manoël-Florisse): Bruno Agar, a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte, and his Malagasy partner (pseudonym Abdallah) married at Sada Town Hall after a 'long and complicated' path — showing the gap between formal French rights and lived reality on this predominantly Muslim island. Same-sex marriage is legal here — a rarity in Africa and the Islamic world — since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975.

Avocat Gay-Friendly directory (French): no LGBT-friendly lawyer is yet referenced in Mayotte — the town list (Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada and others) returns 'we do not yet have a lawyer referenced in your region' — while Paris-based Maître Isabelle Zribi (lawyer at the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, including persons and family law) is listed as available. Evidence of thin local legal-access infrastructure for anyone needing counsel on the island.

Washington Blade op-ed (22 May 2024) by Daniel Digashu and Anna Mmolai-Chalmers of the Southern Africa Litigation Centre: Namibia's Supreme Court in May 2023 ordered the government to recognise same-sex marriages concluded abroad under the Immigration Act, but compliance has failed — immigration officials tell litigant Digashu himself that the ruling covers only case couples (he receives a visitor's visa on every exit), and gender-recognition orders are applied only to named applicants rather than 'all persons'. A hostile parliamentary marriage-bill response and misleading media amplified the non-implementation. Documents the enforcement gap between pro-equality rulings and administrative practice.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Mambaonline (28 May 2018): Out-Right Namibia opened Namibia's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre, Outreach Health, on 17 May (IDAHOT) at 30 Lister St, Windhoek West — HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, mental and sexual/reproductive health services, with plans for legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations. ORN director Friedel Dausab: 'It is a first.' The article notes the colonial-era sodomy law is on the books but not believed used since independence in 1990, and recalls 2016 UN Human Rights Committee recommendations urging SOGI non-discrimination legislation.

Mambaonline (12 December 2018): dozens marched in Windhoek and Swakopmund on 8 December for LGBTI+ Pride — described as the 'biggest pride event' to date in Namibia. Dated evidence of a visible, tolerated public community presence.

Daily Maverick (26 June 2014): a Namibian version of South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters was launched with identical branding (T-shirts, berets) but an explicitly anti-gay stance, unlike the South African original. Documents organised political hostility to LGBT rights in the record's political environment.

BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018): trans women in France are incarcerated per their legal gender marker (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code), typically in all-male facilities facing detainant assault threats, placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework applies to this collectivity's establishments as French law.

Opinion of France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL (25 May 2021): 'persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty — referrals since 2010 on some forty transgender persons plus on-site inspections (Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse; eight trans women and one trans man interviewed). Extends to establishments here as French law applies.

CNN (29 May 2013): reports France's first same-sex wedding following the 2013 marriage-equality law. French marriage law applies to this collectivity — the milestone establishing marriage availability here.

PinkNews (26 August 2012, Joseph McCormick): the French government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge — the legislative path that later extended marriage equality to this collectivity as French law.

Yagg (July 2012, French): 'identité sexuelle' (sexual identity) became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code via the sexual-harassment law — enabling prosecution of discrimination and transphobia as discrimination. French law applies to the collectivity, and the same provision was updated to read 'gender identity' in 2016.

Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: in March 2025 Niger explicitly outlawed same-sex acts for the first time — Article 25 of the junta's Charter of Refoundation bans 'LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior' during the five-year transition following the July 2023 coup. No specific penalties are set yet, but a 2023 draft penal code proposes up to five years for same-sex conduct, 20 years for conducting/officiating/witnessing a same-sex marriage and five years for participating in or financing 'homosexual' organisations. Earlier in 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency Article 276 (up to three years) and the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them; the code fixes age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts versus 13 for different-sex acts.

BBC News live page (December 2022): Niger's lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, moved by MP Nana Djibou Harouna of the southern Maradi region — weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges because no legislation criminalised same-sex relationships. Documents the legislative trail into the 2025 criminalisation.

The Guardian (1 July 2026): at least 40 people have been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men — including high-ranking military officials — imprisoned across Niger following the introduction of a new penal code earlier in 2026, in what campaigners describe as a 'witch-hunt' with a 'toxic' climate; sources also fear an HIV/AIDS resurgence as access to PrEP drugs collapses. Current enforcement evidence for the record.

Agence Nigérienne de Presse (state news agency, French): headline 'Le Niger criminalise la Pratique LGBTQIA+ dans le pays' — official state-press announcement of the criminalisation. Page body was largely navigation content at fetch time; headline finding only.
